text: Lesson 21 gave us an upgrade timeline for a single platform event. Now we zoom out to something that runs continuously underneath that timeline: how often an organization's own teams release their customizations to production, and how that rhythm interacts with everything else happening on the instance.

The DevOps, Testing and Deployment course covered Source Control Integration and external CI/CD pipelines — the mechanics of getting a change out of an update set workflow and into a version-controlled, pipeline-driven process. That answered how a change technically moves from a sandbox to production. This lesson answers a different question: how often should that happen across the whole organization, and who actually decides?

Picture an enterprise instance with three teams. Team A owns a small, low-risk application and ships weekly. Team B owns a large application with many downstream dependents and deliberately ships once a quarter, batching changes for a full regression pass. Team C integrates with an external partner and ships whenever that partner's API changes. All three teams' code lives on the same shared instance, six weeks from a major platform upgrade.

None of those three cadences is wrong on its own. The problem is that they don't exist in isolation. If Team A keeps shipping weekly straight through the upgrade testing window, the pre-upgrade sandbox stops being a stable baseline, because new changes keep landing on top of whatever the upgrade validation was just tested against. If Team B's quarterly release happens to fall inside that same window, its large batch of changes competes for the same limited testing bandwidth as the upgrade itself. Neither team did anything wrong by its own cadence. The collision is a planning failure, not a team failure.

An architect can't just pick whichever cadence is most convenient for one team and force the others onto it. That optimizes for one team's velocity at the expense of the rest, and it gets re-litigated at the next upgrade anyway. The real job is a published release calendar showing every team's planned windows alongside the upgrade schedule, with a negotiated change freeze around the testing period, built with input from every team so the burden doesn't always land on the same one.

Team A's weekly cadence doesn't permanently slow down; it pauses for a defined, communicated window. Team B's quarterly release gets scheduled clear of that window from the start. Next up: technical debt on the platform, which is often exactly what those freeze-window negotiations are quietly protecting against.
